XSYNC USER MANUALSECTION 7

xsync-lessons(7) ​

Lessons

What the first xsync learned from its benchmarks, and what xsync does with it.

IN SHORT ​

Before this C++ version, xsync was written in Rust. That first version ran a long series of measured experiments across a MacBook, two Ryzen workstations, a Raspberry Pi and Windows. Most of its speed came from a handful of big ideas. Most clever-sounding tweaks did almost nothing. And the test machine itself caused fake results more than once.

Do less work per file

Bundling, cloning and checking things once beat every low-level trick.

Measure the machine you sync with

The best thread count changed from 4 to 24 depending on the disk.

Don’t trust one run

The same transfer took 23 s cold and 11 s warm, with no code change.

A FEW BIG IDEAS DID MOST OF THE WORK ​

Each bar is one change v1 tried, measured against the version without it. The blue changes stayed. The gray ones were measured and dropped: even at their best they were within a few percent of doing nothing.

One example: v1 once asked the operating system 3.9 times as often as rsync did, about 25 calls per file instead of 6. Cutting those calls by 44% made it only 13% faster, because creating the files on disk was the real limit. Fewer steps only helps when those steps are what you’re waiting for.

MORE THREADS ISN’T ALWAYS FASTER ​

Copying 10,000 small files locally, Linux kept getting faster all the way to 24 threads. macOS peaked at four or five and then got slower, because its file system handles changes to a folder one at a time. v1’s default of one thread per core was 8–15% slower than the best setting on the Mac.

What xsync does with this: choose the thread count from the kind of disk, not the number of cores. See roadmap item 2.3.

CLONE BIG FILES, COPY SMALL ONES ​

A clone makes a new file that shares storage with the original until either one changes. It sounds free, but on macOS each clone carries a fixed cost. For small files a plain copy is quicker. Past about 12 MiB, cloning wins and keeps winning.

The same idea applies to whole folders: cloning a new folder in one call was 6.3 times faster than cloning its files one by one. On Linux, v1 found the biggest local win by checking once whether the disk supports clones, instead of trying and failing for every file (2.98× faster).

COMPRESSION: SAMPLE FIRST, THEN KEEP IT SIMPLE ​

Compressing data before sending it made a 100,000-file transfer 1.66 times as fast. But data that is already compressed, like photos or archives, only gets slower. v1 compresses a small sample first and sends the rest raw if the sample doesn’t shrink. Going from the default level 3 down to level 1 saved just 5%. Level 9 doubled the time.

Level 3 measured 7.53–7.54 s in the two sessions these numbers come from.

EXTRA CONNECTIONS ONLY HELP BIG FILES ​

Splitting a file across several SSH connections lets more processor cores encrypt at once. That helped for files of 16 MiB and up. For trees of small files it made things slower, and on Windows extra connections cost 1.4–1.5 times the time. Too many connections also run into SSH server limits.

THE NETWORK IS USUALLY THE LIMIT, NOT ENCRYPTION ​

On a gigabit network, which carries about 125 MB/s at most, every SSH cipher v1 tried was within 4% of the others, and SSH matched a raw unencrypted socket. Encryption speed only matters on faster links. There, the default ChaCha20 cipher is much slower than AES on processors with AES hardware.

Measured on one Ryzen 7950X talking to itself, so no network limit applied. The Raspberry Pi 5’s processor has AES instructions too, and on v1’s gigabit link to a Pi the two ciphers tied; roadmap item 3.4 measures it.

THE TEST MACHINE CAN FAKE A RESULT ​

The same transfer to the same server took twice as long on its first runs as it did once the machine had warmed up. Nothing in the code changed.

v1 recorded other ways the environment pretended to be the code:

  • Old binary. One whole experiment measured a stale build and had to be thrown away.
  • Heat. A Raspberry Pi drifted from 18.1 s to 27.1 s over one session, most likely because it slowed itself down as it got hot.
  • Tired disks. On a drive whose fast write cache kept filling up, one setting took anywhere from 61 to 94 seconds.
  • A busy computer. One measurement ran while the machine’s load average was 265.
  • Leftover writes. rsync can exit with 2.4 GB still waiting to reach the disk, so “finished” isn’t the same as “saved”.
  • The network itself. A slow link and a stale IP address both produced fake regressions.

What xsync does with this: every benchmark alternates xsync and rsync, checks every copy byte for byte, records the machine’s state, and repeats each case. See how we measure.

WHAT CARRIES OVER TO XSYNC TODAY ​

Lesson from v1In xsync now
Bundle small files and keep the pipe fullDone: 1 MiB blocks hold many small files, and listing, reading, sending and writing overlap
Clone whole new folders on macOSDone for new folders of files and links, up to 4,096 entries
Check once whether a Linux disk can clonePlanned: roadmap 2.1
Choose threads by disk, not coresPlanned: roadmap 2.3
Compress only what shrinksPlanned: roadmap 3.1
Use extra connections for big files onlyPlanned, only if measurements call for it: roadmap 3.5
Don’t trust a single runDone: paired, verified benchmarks and a CI speed check

SOURCES ​

Every figure links to the v1 files its numbers come from, in the s4njee/xsync repository. Speed-ups are relative to the version without each change on the same machine and data. Charts are drawn with Holochart. The full analysis, with a citation for every number, is in ROADMAP.md.
